newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia euthanasia lobby pressures politicans.
newsitem.headline: Australia euthanasia lobby pressures politicans.

text.p: Australian euthanasia campaigners on Friday stepped up pressure on the national government not to overturn the world's first voluntary euthanasia law, forming a new group to push for nationwide laws allowing assisted suicide.

The new coalition of pro-euthanasia groups, which includes Australia's "Doctor Death" Philip Nitschke, urged the national parliament to heed opinion polls showing overwhelming public support for voluntary euthanasia.

"The majority should rule and an overwhelming majority of Australians support voluntary euthanasia -- around 75 percent according to the latest opinion polls," coalition spokesman David Marr told reporters at a press conference.

Parliament is considering a government member's private motion to use its constitutional powers to overturn the voluntary euthanasia law, which came into effect in the remote outback Northern Territory seven months ago.
Euthanasia is illegal in the rest of Australia, but doctors say the practice occurs unofficially.

Backbencher Kevin Andrews' motion was overwhelmingly approved in the lower house, the House of Representatives, in late 1996 and Marr accused the upper house Senate of trying to now rush the motion through without adequate consideration.
The Senate is expected to vote on the bill in March.
"What we fear is that a sleazy deal has been done to rush a decision on the Andrews Bill through the Senate in a way that shows further contempt for the majority," Marr said.

"When the House of Representatives ignored these majority views it was a real blow to democracy. Senators now have the opportunity to prove that not all politicians are frigthened of militant minorities," he said.
Political leaders, including Prime Minister John Howard and opposition Labor leader Kim Beazley, have joined religious, Aboriginal and medical groups in supporting the Andrews Bill.
Marr said the new coalition, which does not yet have a formal name, would lobby the national and state governments and campaign during elections in support of new euthanasia laws.

The controversial Northern Territory legislation has already survived a raft of political and legal challenges. But uncertainty about its fate has meant only three people have died under the law, all with Nitschke's help.
Nitschke, dubbed "Doctor Death" by anti-euthanasia lobbyists, told reporters on Thursday the controversy over the law created great uncertainty and confusion for his dying patients.

"There's certainly apprehension among those who have contacted me...and a great deal of anxiety and apprehension about what the Senate vote will mean," Nitschke said. "It's an impossible position that these people have been put in."

Under the law, terminally ill patients can choose to kill themselves with lethal pills or an injection if they meet strict criteria and obtain the signatures of a doctor, psychiatrist and a specialiast in the disease from which they suffer.
